entries.content:
ibm-granite/granite-speech-5.0-470m-turboctc

Automatic Speech Recognition • 0.5B • Updated • 59.3k • 80

Granite Switch 4.1: Chat, Decisions, and Speech from One Endpoint

Enterprise Article

Granite Switchproject enables a modular approach to model development. Now Granite Switch 4.1 models, armed with a Decision adapter and the fastest ASR model on the OpenASR leaderboard, can move efficiently between natural-language responses, general and specialized decisions, and speech-to-text tasks—all from one hosted endpoint.

Specifically, Granite-Switch-4.1-8B and -30B models are configured to include:

  • A new Decision aLoRA for general-purpose decision-making (e.g. v1/systemone),
  • A specialized Guardian aLoRA that, on average, outperforms Jev 1.13, Microsoft-Decision-1, GPT-Luna-Decisions, and Clef-Flash on safety-related decision tasks, and
  • Granite-Speech-5.0-Turbo-CTC, the fastest ASR model on the OpenASR Leaderboard, embedded for use in transcription tasks.

All three of these technologies (along with the underlying base model) are composed into one model, taking up approximately the same amount of VRAM on a GPU as the base model would by itself. That means more capabilities with fewer GPUs.

And because the Switch adapters were built as cache-efficient Activated LoRAs, the KV cache created from a base model generation can be reused for any subsequent adapter-based decisions. Combined with our team's recent vLLM contributions to speed up low rank adapter inferencing, as well as a co-located ASR encoder, Granite Switch 4.1 models can switch between a chat request and a decision request and a spoken request, with blazing fast speeds.

Check out our Speech-to-Decisions HF space where granite-switch-4.1-8b transcribes audio, generates summaries, screens for harmful content, and tests 15 other user-defined flags—all running on a single endpoint in real time.

Granite Libraries: The OG Decision Models

Decision models aren’t new. Our previous release of Granite Libraries features a repository of specialized “decision model” adapters and other specialized task adapters that can be composed into custom Granite Switch models. And while Jev and other closed decision models focus on generality, we’ve found that many of our specialized granitelib adapters can outperform generalists on specialized classification tasks.

Compare granitelib adapters with generalist decision models when evaluated on specialized classification tasks.

Because adapters share the base model's KV cache, adding specialists alongside a generalist decision adapter costs almost nothing. You get broad coverage from the generalist and higher accuracy from specialists on the tasks you care about.

In a “Race” between Granite-Switch-4.1-30B (frozen base Granite + 4 specialized aLoRAs) and Jev-27B (frozen base Qwen model + 1 generic decision LoRA), Granite-Switch-4.1-30B was able to complete a real world, 5-step RAG workflow much faster than its competitor.

Compose and Extend Your Own Granite Switch Model

Granite-Switch-4.1-8B and -30B are released with “batteries included”. They are Granite Switch models that we compiled with a predefined set of helpful adapters. But you don’t need to use our version. Anyone can compose their own Granite Switch model, mixing and matching adapters from Granite Libraries to best meet their needs.

Moving forward, we see tremendous opportunity for the community to compose and extend Granite Switch models with custom and third party adapters. We plan to release an Adapter SDK for training adapters in Mellea, along side other tutorials and Granite Switch support. These adapters could be specialized classification adapters to augment decision-based workflows or adapters for specialized language tasks. You could even use custom adapters to teach a 3B parameter version of Granite to play the classic game Doom.

Similarly to Jev, our custom 3B parameter Granite Switch model made split second decisions to navigate the Doom game, but was able to do so at 60 - 100 decisions / second, compared to Jev’s reported 10 decisions / second.1 Unlike Jev, this Granite Switch model can also narrate and respond to your questions while it is playing.

Accessible from anywhere

Coming in 8b and 30b sizes, Granite Switch 4.1 can fit wherever your workload runs. The model runs in vllm with a plug-in (see Granite Switch repo below), and has native inference support in 

llama.cpp
and downstream platforms which allows the model to seamlessly swap in for 
/v1/systemone
API calls anywhere they're used, while also servicing traditional chat calls, all with a shared prefix cache.

Resources for Getting Started

  • Granite Switch 4.1 Model Cards
  • Speech-to-Decisions Demo
  • Granite Switch GitHub Repo
  • Original Granite Switch and Granite Libraries Release Blog
  • Create your own aLoRA v LoRA race on Colab.

Footnotes

1 https://typesafe.ai/blog/introducing-system-one-models-and-jev

entries.title: Welcome Muse Spark Open: open-weight frontier multimodal mixture-of-experts model from Meta
entries.content:
meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B

Image-Text-to-Text • 822B • Updated • 1.81k • 521

Welcome Muse Spark Open: open-weight frontier multimodal mixture-of-experts model from Meta

Update on GitHub

Following Muse Glimmer, Muse Spark Open introduces a mixture-of-experts architecture at a much larger scale, and the most capable US open-weights model to date.

Meta trained Muse Spark Open for agentic coding: reading a codebase, writing and debugging code, and calling tools. It also takes images, audio, and video as input, so the same model can read a screenshot, listen to a voice note, or watch a screen recording while it works on your code. This post shows you how to run it, how to fine-tune it, and what we built with it. Find all the models here.

Overall Capabilities and Architecture

Meta describes Muse Spark Open as a coding-optimized model trained on real developer workflows such as multi-file refactors and long debugging sessions. Muse Spark Open is an agentic focused model that plans, acts, observes, and self-corrects over long tasks, including browsing the web with images.

FeatureMuse Spark Open
Model size~816B total parameters; ~42B active per token
Expert routing256 experts per MoE layer; 8 selected per token
InputsText, images, audio, and video
OutputText
Context windowUp to 1M tokens
Checkpoint formatsBF16 and NVFP4

The checkpoint repositories are Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B and Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4.

Muse Spark Open is the full-size model of the Muse series of models. Muse Glimmer, which Meta released in August, is a small dense model from the same series, ideal for running locally. Both models use the same tokenizer and vocabulary. The chat template follows the Muse Glimmer template, with additions for the new modalities. In Muse Spark Open the input embedding and the output layer are separate matrices of about 1.66B parameters each.

Mixture of Experts

The language model has 62 layers and a hidden dimension of 8192. Each layer has 128 query heads and 16 key-value heads (grouped-query attention). Each head has 64 dimensions. The attention block has an output gate and an output normalization layer. The model also applies normalization to the queries and the keys (QK-norm). Each block combines its input and its output through a learned residual gate, not through a plain sum.

Muse Glimmer uses one dense feed-forward network in each layer. Muse Spark Open replaces this dense network with a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) block. Each MoE block has 256 experts, and a router selects 8 experts for each token. Each expert is a feed-forward network that projects from 8192 to 4096 dimensions and back to 8192, then applies its own normalization to its output. The experts hold ~97% of the total model parameters.

Only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 42B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of an 816B-parameter model, but runs at the much faster speed of a 42B model. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1.5 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores the parameters in 4-bit precision with negligible loss in accuracy, specifically for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs. In transformers, the BF16 checkpoint runs across 4 nodes of 8 H200 GPUs with tensor parallelism (TP=32) and the NVFP4 runs on a single B200 node. If you want to deploy Muse Spark Open, check out the 

llama.cpp
, vLLM, and SGLang recipes below.

Perception Encoder

A perception encoder converts images and video frames into tokens for the language model, just like Muse Glimmer. The encoder has 1.8B parameters, 50 layers, a hidden dimension of 1536, and 16 attention heads. It splits each image into 14×14 patches and produces features with 4096 dimensions. Position information comes from learned absolute embeddings and 2D RoPE. The feed-forward network in each layer uses LayerNorm and GELU. Every fourth layer and the last layer use full attention, and the other layers use sparse attention.

Muse Glimmer 30B uses an encoder with the same architecture. The design follows the Perception Encoder work from Meta. Video input goes through the same encoder as images.

Audio Encoder

Muse Spark Open accepts audio as input through its audio encoder. An audio tokenizer converts the audio into tokens, and the chat template marks the audio position with 

<|audio|>
tokens. The encoder emits one audio token every 80 ms, which yields 12.5 tokens per second. So let’s say, you have an audio of 10 seconds, the number of input audio tokens would be 125. The encoder itself is a convolutional pyramid where each stage consists of a patch embedder of different patch sizes and 2 convolutional blocks of 1d kernels of size 7 with stride of 1. These stages are repeated for patch sizes of [16, 6, 5, 4]. At the end of the final stage, the temporal frames are fed to a final block of RMSNorm → linear projection → RMSNorm.

Long Context

The context window is 1M tokens at inference. The configuration sets 

max_position_embeddings
to 1,048,576. This includes image, video, and audio tokens in the same window as text.

Grouped-query attention keeps the KV cache small for a model of this size. Each token adds 2 × 16 heads × 64 dimensions × 62 layers = 126,976 values to the cache. In BF16, this is about 250 KB per token and about 266 GB for a full 1M-token context.

Inference Support

Transformers

The Muse Spark Open implementation provides 

MuseSparkForConditionalGeneration
for text generation from multimodal inputs and 
MuseSparkProcessor
for preparing conversations. The processor combines the tokenizer, image and video processors, audio feature extractor, and chat template.

Use a 

DistributedConfig
to configure the parallelism settings. 
tp_size
is the number of devices across which the dense layers are sharded, and 
ep_size
is the number of devices across which the experts are distributed.

You can initialize the model and processor as follows.

import os

from transformers import AutoModelForMultimodalLM, AutoTokenizer, DistributedConfig

distributed_config = DistributedConfig(
    tp_size=int(os.environ["WORLD_SIZE"]),
    ep_size=int(os.environ["WORLD_SIZE"]),
)

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B
")
model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained(
    "meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B",
    distributed_config=distributed_config,
)

messages = [
    {"role": "user", "content": "Explain in one sentence why the sky is usually blue."},
]
inputs = tokenizer.apply_chat_template(
    messages,
    reasoning_effort="medium",  # default: xhigh, options: low/medium/high/xhigh
    add_generation_prompt=True,
    tokenize=True,
    return_dict=True,
    return_tensors="pt",
).to(model.device).to(model.dtype)

input_len = inputs["input_ids"].shape[-1]

outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=2000)

Text-only Inference

Prepare the conversation, then pass the messages to 

processor.apply_chat_template
, enabling 
add_generation_prompt=True
, 
tokenize=True
, 
return_dict=True
, and 
return_tensors="pt"
. Pass the processor output to 
model.generate
and decode the newly generated tokens, excluding the input prefix. The processor has a lever for the reasoning effort, mapping symbolic levels (low/medium/high/xhigh) to the integers the model itself accepts (16, 64, 256, 512). Note that turning off reasoning is not possible with Muse Spark Open, so keep the model reasoning at “low” if you want to consume less tokens to solve an easier task. You can also set a numeric effort by including a line like 
Reasoning strength: 1
in the system prompt.
messages = [
    {"role": "system", "content": "You should only answer with a number."},
    {"role": "user", "content": "What is 17 * 23?"},
]

inputs = processor.apply_chat_template(
    messages,
    add_generation_prompt=True,
    tokenize=True,
    return_dict=True,
    return_tensors="pt",
    reasoning_effort="high", # options:low/medium/high/xhigh
).to(model.device).to(model.dtype)

output = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=2000)
generated_tokens = output[0][inputs["input_ids"].shape[1] :]
print(processor.decode(generated_tokens, skip_special_tokens=False))

Images and Text

The Muse Spark Open processor expands each image marker into the number of patch tokens required by the processed image, surrounded by image boundary tokens. This expansion keeps the text positions aligned with the visual features passed to the model. The processor also handles multiple images within a single prompt.

image_url = (
    "https://huggingface.co/datasets/merve/vl-test-suite/"
    "resolve/main/pills.jpg"
)
messages = [
    {
        "role": "user",
        "content": [
            {
                "type": "image",
                "image": image_url,
            },
            {
                "type": "text",
                "text": "Do any of the components in this supplement interact?",
            },
        ],
    },
]

inputs = processor.apply_chat_template(
    messages,
    tokenize=True,
    add_generation_prompt=True,
    reasoning_effort="medium",
    return_dict=True,
    return_tensors="pt",
).to(model.device).to(model.dtype)
input_len = inputs["input_ids"].shape[-1]

outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=2000)
response = processor.decode(outputs[0][input_len:], skip_special_tokens=False)

processor.parse_response(response)

Video Inference

Video prompts include frame timing as well as visual content. The processor handles videos with audios in them (which is an upgrade from Muse Glimmer thanks to the audio encoder). The processor downsamples video frames and audio to align frames together. By default, videos are sampled to 2 FPS, capped at 96 frames. You can modify this by setting the fps of the video processor:

processor.video_processor.fps = 4.0

As a general rule of thumb, videos are frames in temporal sequence, and the more you downsample, the more you will lose frames in between specific events, so you need to keep fps high if you want more accurate generations. However, there’s a trade-off because you will require more memory and increase latency for prefill. The frames are interleaved with text input that states timestamps (e.g. “Time: 3.5s”). To enable passing in videos with audio, pass 

load_audio_from_video=True
to 
apply_chat_template
.

Preserve the video's metadata when preparing inputs with 

return_metadata=True
so the processor can assign the correct framerate.
import torch

messages = [
    {
        "role": "user",
        "content": [
            {
                "type": "text",
                "text": (
                    "Describe what happens in this video. "
                    "Use timestamps and include relevant speech or sounds."
                ),
            },
            {
                "type": "video",
                "url": "https://huggingface.co/datasets/merve/vlm_test_images/resolve/main/ramen.mp4"
            },
        ],
    }
]

inputs = processor.apply_chat_template(
    messages,
    add_generation_prompt=True,
    tokenize=True,
    return_dict=True,
    return_tensors="pt",
    load_audio_from_video=True,
    return_metadata=True,
).to(model.device).to(model.dtype)

with torch.inference_mode():
    output_ids = model.generate(
        **inputs,
        max_new_tokens=256,
        do_sample=False,
    )

generated_ids = output_ids[:, inputs["input_ids"].shape[1] :]
response = processor.batch_decode(
    generated_ids,
    skip_special_tokens=True,
)[0]

print(response)

Audio Inference

The Muse Spark Open audio tower consumes a raw waveform. The processor expects mono audio at 24 kHz and pads the waveform to a multiple of 1,920 samples, corresponding to one audio embedding per 80 milliseconds. Audio supplied directly to the processor at another sample rate must first be resampled. You can do this by using the 

load_audio
util of transformers. 
load_audio
uses torchcodec, librosa or torchaudio backends, so make sure to have one of these installed locally before running inference.

If you want to simply use 

apply_chat_template
with messages though, this is all handled for you under the hood:
import torch
from transformers import AutoProcessor, AutoModelForMultimodalLM

model_id = "meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B"
processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id)

model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained(model_id).eval()

messages = [
    {
        "role": "user",
        "content": [
            {
                "type": "audio",
                "url": "https://huggingface.co/buckets/huggingface/audio-samples/resolve/bbaudio_question_39.mp3",
            },
            {
                "type": "text",
                "text": "Answer the question.",
            },
        ],
    }
]

# Downloads the audio, decodes it as mono, resamples it to 24 kHz, pads it, creates input_values_mask, and expands the audio placeholders.
inputs = processor.apply_chat_template(
    messages,
    add_generation_prompt=True,
    tokenize=True,
    return_dict=True,
    return_tensors="pt",
    load_audio_backend="auto",
).to(model.device).to(model.dtype)

with torch.inference_mode():
    output_ids = model.generate(
        **inputs,
        max_new_tokens=128,
        do_sample=False,
    )

# Decode only newly generated tokens
prompt_length = inputs["input_ids"].shape[1]
generated_text = processor.batch_decode(
    output_ids[:, prompt_length:],
    skip_special_tokens=True,
)

print(generated_text[0])

The processor inserts the matching number of audio tokens between audio boundary markers. It also returns a mask identifying real samples, allowing the model to exclude padded audio embeddings.

Tool Calling

Muse Spark Open can do text-only and multimodal tool calling. You can make the model call tools as follows.

from transformers import AutoProcessor, AutoModelForMultimodalLM

MODEL_ID = "meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B"

# Load model
processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(MODEL_ID)
model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained(
    MODEL_ID,
    dtype="auto",
    device_map="auto"
)

tools = [
    {
        "type": "function",
        "function": {
            "name": "weather.get",
            "description": "Get the current weather for a city.",
            "parameters": {
                "type": "object",
                "properties": {
                    "city": {"type": "string"},
                },
                "required": ["city"],
            },
        },
    }
]


messages = [
    {
        "role": "user",
        "content": [
            {"type": "image", "image": "https://huggingface.co/datasets/merve/vl-test-suite/resolve/main/SF.png"},
            {"type": "text", "text": "I'm going to the city in this picture. What clothes should I wear?"},
        ],
    },
]

inputs = processor.apply_chat_template(
    messages,
    tools=tools,
    tokenize=True,
    return_dict=True,
    return_tensors="pt",
    add_generation_prompt=True,
    reasoning_strength="high"
).to(model.device).to(model.dtype)

input_len = inputs["input_ids"].shape[-1]
outputs = model.generate(**inputs)
response = processor.parse_response(
      completion,
      prefix=inputs["input_ids"][0],
      tools=tools,
  )
print(response)

Muse Spark Open uses a channel-based chat template (Harmony, first introduced by gpt-oss). Note that you don’t have to know about the internals, but it’s useful to check the channels the model routes to, in case you get low quality outputs. In the input message below:

<|begin_of_text|>
  <|start|>system<|message|>
  You are a helpful AI assistant.
  Knowledge cutoff: 2026-01-04.
  Current date: ...
  ...
  <|eot|>
  <|start|>user<|message|>...
  <|eot|>
  <|start|>assistant


<|start|>assistant
is intentionally left open, it’s the model that chooses recipient with 
to=
. The model has different recipients, e.g. 
self
asks the model to reason, 
to=self<|message|>the model reasons here<|eom|> # reasoning
<|start|>assistant to=user<|message|>final answer<|eot|> # final answer


self
is for reasoning, 
commentary
are comments before and between tool calls visible to the end user, 
user
is the final response.

Tool-call routing is parsed as follows (assuming you have passed 
tools
to 
apply_chat_template
:
<|start|>assistant to=weather.get<|message|>
  
  
  San Francisco
  
  
  <|eot|>

Llama.cpp

Muse Spark 2-bit running on Llama Server

Muse Spark Open is integrated in llama.cpp and comes in the prebuilt binaries. You can install this with following command:

curl -LsSf https://llama.app/install.sh | sh

You can start the server as follows with quant suffix attached to model ID:

llama serve -hf ggml-org/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-GGUF:Q2_K

The repository containing quants is here. Once the server has started, you can head to localhost:9931 to chat with the built-in WebUI. From the web UI you can add audio and images for inference and adjust the reasoning lever.

Note that turning off reasoning is not possible with Muse Spark Open, so keep the model reasoning at “low” if you want to consume less tokens to solve an easier task.

We tested quants on Mac M3 Ultra (512GB). An imatrix-calibrated 2-bit quant runs at 18 tokens/s, with plenty of room free for the KV cache (304 GB used by the model).

You can also query the server as follows. Feel free to check out the API reference for multimodality, tool calls and more. 

## Text-only inference
curl http://localhost:8080/v1/chat/completions \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d '{
        "messages": [
            {"role": "system", "content": "You are a helpful assistant."},
            {"role": "user", "content": "Write a limerick about python exceptions"}
        ]
    }'

## Image-text inference
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" -H "Authorization: Bearer " \
  -d '{"model":"muse-spark-open","messages":[{"role":"user","content":[
        {"type":"text","text":"What is in this image?"},
        {"type":"image_url","image_url":{"url":"data:image/png;base64,..."}}
      ]}],"temperature":0}'

## Audio-text inference
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" -H "Authorization: Bearer " \
  -d '{"model":"muse-spark-open","messages":[{"role":"user","content":[
        {"type":"text","text":"Transcribe this audio."},
        {"type":"input_audio","input_audio":{"data":"data:audio/wav;base64,..."}}
      ]}],"temperature":0}'

llama.cpp team ships different quantized versions. We have tested Q2_K, Q4_K_S and Q_8 on Apple Silicon chips. You can run each quant by adding the quant id as suffix, 

llama serve -hf ggml-org/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B:Q2_K
.

SGLang

The Muse Spark Open integration for SGLang supports text, image, audio, and video inputs. The NVFP4 reference configuration runs across four GB300 GPUs.

From the SGLang integration environment, download the checkpoint from the Hugging Face Hub and start the server:

export MODEL_ID=meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4
export CKPT="$(hf download "$MODEL_ID")"

SGLANG_FLASHINFER_NVFP4_PER_TOKEN_ACTIVATION=1 \
uv run sglang_meta serve \
  --model-path "$CKPT" \
  --served-model-name "$MODEL_ID" \
  --quantization modelopt_fp4 \
  --moe-runner-backend flashinfer_trtllm \
  --tp-size 4 \
  --ep-size 4 \
  --port 30000

The checkpoint includes the chat template, which we pass explicitly. The launcher configures the Muse reasoning and tool-call parsers.

Send a request through the OpenAI-compatible API:

curl http://localhost:30000/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "model": "meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4",
    "messages": [{
      "role": "user",
      "content": "Explain how a mixture-of-experts model works."
    }],
    "max_tokens": 2048
  }'

The response separates the reasoning trace in 

reasoning_content
from the final answer in 
content
.

vLLM

The Muse Spark Open reference integration for vLLM supports text and image inputs with the NVFP4 checkpoint that require blackwell series GPUs.

After installing the reference plugin and its dependencies, download the checkpoint from the Hugging Face Hub and launch the server:

export MODEL_ID=meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4
export CKPT="$(hf download "$MODEL_ID")"

VLLM_ALLOW_LONG_MAX_MODEL_LEN=1 \
VLLM_PLUGINS=musespark1x_models,ptq_nvfp4 \
vllm serve "$CKPT" \
  --served-model-name "$MODEL_ID" \
  --tokenizer-mode musespark1x \
  --config-format auto \
  --load-format internal_safetensor \
  --tensor-parallel-size 4 \
  --enable-expert-parallel \
  --max-model-len 131072 \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.92 \
  --reasoning-parser musespark1x \
  --tool-call-parser musespark1x \
  --enable-auto-tool-choice \
  --port 8000

This configuration sets a 128K-token serving context. The plugin supplies the model implementation, checkpoint loader, and reasoning and tool-call parsers.

Send a request using the same Hub model ID:

curl http://localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "model": "meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4",
    "messages": [{
      "role": "user",
      "content": "Explain how a mixture-of-experts model works."
    }],
    "max_tokens": 2048
  }'

MLX

Muse Spark Open is available in oMLX and mlx-lm today. oQ quants optimized for oMLX are available in 3-bit and 4-bit, ready to use right away.

We tested the oQ3e quant on an M3 Ultra (512 GB). The model takes about 344 GB, leaving room for the KV cache, and runs at about 225 tok/s prefill and 21 tok/s generation with a 1024-token prompt and 128 generated tokens.

Once you download the model through the oMLX interface, you can chat with it in the built-in chat UI. From the chat UI you can add images and adjust the reasoning effort on the fly, from low to xhigh. The model’s reasoning shows up as a collapsible thinking block, separate from the final answer.

Note that it's not possible to turn reasoning off, and the default (Auto) uses xhigh. Set it to “low” if you want to use fewer tokens on easier tasks.

The language model is also available in this PR of the official mlx-lm repository. You can run it on the same high-quality oQ3e quant like this:

mlx_lm.generate --model mlx-community/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-oQ3e \
  --prompt "Explain convolutional networks like I am 5" \
  --max-tokens 5000

This is a big model, even the 3-bit quantization requires more than 256 GB of RAM, as explained above. You can also run distributed inference across multiple computers, please refer to the documentation for details.

Deploying Muse Spark Open with Inference Endpoints

You can deploy Muse Spark Open on Inference Endpoints with a pre-validated SGLang recipe for the NVFP4 variant which runs on either 8 × NVIDIA RTX Pro 6000 98 GB with 131072 context length, or with 8 x NVIDIA H200 141GB if you want 1048576 context length instead.

To deploy, run one command with the Hugging Face CLI:

hf endpoints catalog deploy --repo meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 --name muse-spark

Or open endpoints.huggingface.co/new/meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 and select Create Endpoint.

The endpoint exposes an OpenAI-compatible API with both Chat Completions API at 

/v1/chat/completions
and Responses API at 
/v1/responses
.
curl "https://.endpoints.huggingface.cloud/v1/chat/completions" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $HF_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "model": "meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4",
    "messages": [{
      "role": "user",
      "content": [
        {"type": "image_url", "image_url": {"url": "https://huggingface.co/datasets/merve/vl-test-suite/resolve/main/pills.jpg"}},
        {"type": "text", "text": "Do any of the components in this supplement interact?"}
      ]
    }],
    "chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": false}
  }'

Any OpenAI-compatible client works with the same URL and your Hugging Face token as the API key.

Fine-tuning with TRL

You can fine-tune the 816B checkpoint with the TRL 

SFTTrainer
. This section shows how we fine-tuned it with TRL on 8 nodes of 8 H100 GPUs. The recipe trains LoRA adapters on the attention layers. The experts stay frozen. The full script is in the TRL examples.

First, we need to split the model across 64 GPU devices. Given the large size of the model, we need to parallelize it across multiple axes. We shard the model with FSDP and split the experts across GPUs, using 

DistributedConfig
, which tells 
transformers
how to split the model when it loads:
from transformers.distributed import DistributedConfig

distributed_config = DistributedConfig(fsdp_size=64, ep_size=8)

In the snippet above, 

fsdp_size=64
shards the model across all 64 GPUs with FSDP2, and 
ep_size=8
splits the 256 experts of each layer into 8 groups. Transformers sends each token to the GPU that holds its expert, so each GPU trains on its own slice of the batch.

Now, we can configure the 

SFTConfig
for our training run. We’ve performed a simple task here to adapt the model’s chat template on an open source dataset, but you could apply it to your own use case.
import torch
from datasets import load_dataset
from peft import LoraConfig
from transformers.distributed import DistributedConfig
from trl import SFTConfig, SFTTrainer

train_dataset = load_dataset("allenai/tulu-3-sft-mixture", split="train[:500000]")

training_args = SFTConfig(
    output_dir="muse-spark-lora-sft",
    model_init_kwargs={"dtype": torch.bfloat16, "distributed_config": DistributedConfig(fsdp_size=64, ep_size=8)},
    per_device_train_batch_size=1,
    max_steps=500,
    max_length=2048,
    packing=True,
    save_only_model=True,
    logging_steps=1,
    report_to="trackio",
)

trainer = SFTTrainer(
    model="meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B",
    args=training_args,
    train_dataset=train_dataset,
    peft_config=LoraConfig(r=16, lora_alpha=32, target_modules=["q_proj", "k_proj", "v_proj", "o_proj"]),
)
trainer.train()

The core parts here are 

packing=True
which joins examples into 2048-token sequences without padding. A block-diagonal mask keeps the examples separate. 
save_only_model=True
saves the adapter and no optimizer state, because the trainer cannot resume a model that was sharded at load time. 
LoraConfig
targets the four attention projections and the 256 experts of each layer stay frozen.

Then we can run this command across each node:

torchrun --nnodes 8 --nproc_per_node 8 --rdzv_backend c10d --rdzv_endpoint "$MASTER_IP:29700" sft_muse_spark_open.py

We trained for 500 steps, which took about 2 hours on 64 H100s, at about 8,000 tokens per second. Mean token accuracy rose from 72% to 84% and the loss fell from 1.26 to 0.57, which signals a good fine-tuning run.

Demos

Muse Spark Open is a coding and agentic model. We wanted to see that for ourselves, so we tried a mixture of multi-modal and agentic tasks that use the model's image and audio inputs. Everything below is something you can run or fork.

3D Asset Generator

We combined 2-bit quantized Muse Spark open (served on llama.cpp) with the Pi coding agent to generate and iteratively improve 3D assets in Three.js. You can find the prompt here, as the model is quantized it requires a bit more steering. We get 18 TPS on llama.cpp on Mac Ultra.

We initially describe the asset, and Pi uses the model to generate Three.js code for the asset, renders the result in a browser, and captures screenshots from multiple angles. It then sends those images back to the same model on llama server for visual feedback. Pi uses that feedback to edit the code and repeats the process.

Browser Interactions with OpenEnv and Hugging Face Sandbox

We tested Spark on computer use tasks and were amazed by the performance, so we have built a lean demo that also serves to teach you how a computer use agent works. You can also further customize this for your needs. This is both an educational example and something you can run in a few lines. You can find it here.

Muse Spark NVFP4 Browser Agent with OpenEnv and HF Sandboxes

Hugging Face Sandboxes are sandboxes built on Hugging Face Jobs for easy code execution. The demo consists of three components:

  • Muse Spark Open served with Inference Endpoints,
  • OpenEnv wrapping web driver actions with helium and selenium (click, type, scroll etc) defining browser environment’s reset, step, observation, termination interface,
  • Chromium web browser

where the remote sandbox contains the environment and the browser as illustrated below.

You can easily try this with a few steps, described in the example. Start Inference Endpoint with Muse Spark Open (NVFP4 works well too!), add your endpoint URL as environmental variable, publish your OpenEnv server in Spaces and also provide that, then you can run the agent loop. Muse Spark Open sees the previous actions, system prompt, url and the screenshot of the browser to take an action, and nothing else (no DOM, no HTML code, nothing) so it’s a truly multimodal browser demo.

Call your Browser

Finally, we wanted to push Spark’s agentic multimodality to the limits, so we set up this space that combines the model’s audio, image, and agentic properties into a browser agent. We give the model a general description of a thing we need and it interacts with the integrated browser to find options on Amazon.

Muse Spark Open takes the voice input and reasons over the type of product that meets the descriptions, searches for it on Amazon, and selects the most appropriate based on criteria.

Wrapping Up

Muse Spark Open is a full-size open-weight model from the Muse series. Start with the BF16 or NVFP4 checkpoint, or try one of the great 

llama.cpp quants
. If you build something with Muse Spark Open, share it, and tell us in the repository’s discussions.

entries.title: Welcome FLUX.3 Image Klein in Diffusers
entries.content:
black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein

Image-to-Image • 6B • Updated • 52.3k • 463

Welcome FLUX.3 Image Klein in Diffusers: The latest open image generation model from Black Forest Labs

Update on GitHub

Black Forest LabsFLUX.3 Image Klein is here, and it runs in Diffusers from day one. One model does text-to-image and multi-reference image-to-image, and it adds something new, the layout control. You write bounding boxes into the prompt to say where each part of the image should go, or which parts of a reference image to move.

Both open checkpoints are in the FLUX.3 Image Klein collection:

CheckpointWhat it isDefaults
black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein
 Time step distilled, for fast inference16 steps, no CFG
black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein-base
 Base model50 steps, CFG

You can head on to the Hugging Face space and generate some images right now!

TL;DR

  • One model for text-to-image, multi-reference image-to-image, and bounding-box layout control.
  • The distilled checkpoint makes a 1024 × 1024 image in about 2 seconds on an H100.
  • NVFP4 and FP8 weights load with 
    from_single_file
    , for smaller GPUs.
  • LoRA training scripts for both text-to-image and image editing.
  • Ships as a Modular Diffusers pipeline, so you can pop blocks out or add your own.

Contents

Getting started

Install the latest 

diffusers
and 
transformers
(for the Qwen3-VL text encoder):
pip install -U diffusers transformers

Load the distilled checkpoint and generate an image:

import torch
from diffusers import ModularPipeline

pipe = ModularPipeline.from_pretrained("black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein")
pipe.load_components(dtype=torch.bfloat16)
pipe.to("cuda")

pipe(prompt="a red fox", output="images")[0].save("fox.png")

What FLUX.3 can do

Text-to-image

FLUX.3 responds best to a full scene description with the subject, the setting, the light, the composition, and the style. The official prompting guide from Black Forest Labs has more tips. The distilled checkpoint generates a 

1024 × 1024
image in 
16
steps by default. Pass 
height
, 
width
, or 
num_inference_steps
to change them.
prompt = (
    "A wide-angle wildlife photograph of a red fox standing alert in a snow-covered forest clearing at golden hour. "
    "The fox is centered in the frame, its thick orange winter coat contrasting with the fresh white snow, breath "
    "visible in the cold air. Snow-laden pine trees fill the softly blurred background, and low warm sunlight rakes "
    "across the scene from the left, casting long blue shadows."
)

fox = pipe(
    prompt=prompt,
    generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(0),
    output="images"
)[0]
fox.save("fox.png")

Image-to-image

Pass a reference image (or more) with the 

image
argument. Write the prompt as a caption of the image you want, with the change included.
prompt = (
    "The same red fox in the same snow-covered forest clearing, now at night under a full moon: cool blue "
    "moonlight, deep shadows, stars visible through the pine branches, the fox's eyes catching the light."
)
night = pipe(
    prompt=prompt,
    image=fox, # from the previous text to image example
    generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(0),
    output="images",
)[0]
night.save("night.png")

With several references, refer to them in the prompt as

,
, ... in the order they are passed to 
image
:
red_fox = pipe(prompt="a red fox", generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(0), output="images")[0]
bench = pipe(prompt="a wooden bench", generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(0), output="images")[0]

combined = pipe(
    prompt="The fox from  sitting on the wooden bench from  in a snowy setting.",
    image=[red_fox, bench],
    output="images",
)[0]

combined.save("combined.png")

Layout control

Add a JSON list of regions after the caption. Each region has an 

id
, a 
bbox
, and a 
desc
, and the caption mentions it as
.

Boxes are written as 

[y_min, x_min, y_max, x_max]
, y first, on a 0–1000 scale. Because the scale is normalized, the same box works at any image size.

Placing regions in a new image 

layout_prompt = (
    "Minimalist graphic illustration featuring a black silhouette of a person  centered against a "
    "solid, vibrant chartreuse background . The figure is captured in a dynamic, mid-stride running "
    "pose, facing toward the left side of the frame. "
    '[{"id": "background_1", "bbox": [0, 0, 1000, 1000], "desc": "A flat field of neon yellow-green with a subtle '
    'paper texture and fine, organic grain."}, {"id": "silhouette_1", "bbox": [150, 150, 850, 850], "desc": "A '
    "black silhouette of a person in motion, made of dense stippled ink. The leading edges are solid; the trailing "
    'arm and leg dissolve into coarse square pixels and scattered dots."}]'
)

runner = pipe(prompt=layout_prompt, generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(0), output="images")[0]

Moving regions within a reference image

For edits, each region says where its content comes from (

src_bbox
in the reference) and where it goes (
tgt_bbox
in the output). A region with the same two boxes stays where it is.

This example moves the knitted knight up and to the left, and pins the backdrop, the cliff, the needle, the dragon, and the fire:

from diffusers.utils import load_image

knight_image = load_image("knight_orig.png")
edit_prompt = (
    "In , move the miniature grey amigurumi knight figure  upwards and to the left along the "
    "yarn cliff . Keep the rest of the image completely unchanged, preserving the blurred yarn backdrop "
    ", the large knitted dragon , and the fiery orange thread . "
    '[{"id": "knight_1", "from": "ref_image_0", "src_bbox": [500, 150, 850, 350], "tgt_bbox": [194, 55, 544, 255], '
    '"desc": "A miniature amigurumi knight crocheted from thick grey woolen yarn."}, '
    '{"id": "backdrop_1", "from": "ref_image_0", "src_bbox": [0, 0, 1000, 1000], "tgt_bbox": [0, 0, 1000, 1000], '
    '"desc": "A soft, out-of-focus backdrop of cream and indigo knitted yarn."}, '
    '{"id": "cliff_1", "from": "ref_image_0", "src_bbox": [300, 0, 1000, 450], "tgt_bbox": [300, 0, 1000, 450], '
    '"desc": "A steep cliff of stacked yarn skeins in mustard, terracotta, and indigo."}, '
    '{"id": "needle_1", "from": "ref_image_0", "src_bbox": [420, 250, 550, 450], "tgt_bbox": [420, 250, 550, 450], '
    '"desc": "An oversized polished steel tapestry needle."}, '
    '{"id": "dragon_1", "from": "ref_image_0", "src_bbox": [100, 600, 950, 1000], "tgt_bbox": [100, 600, 950, 1000], '
    '"desc": "A large, fluffy knitted dragon in terracotta and mustard yarn."}, '
    '{"id": "fire_1", "from": "ref_image_0", "src_bbox": [350, 400, 650, 650], "tgt_bbox": [350, 400, 650, 650], '
    '"desc": "Curled puffs of fiery orange angora thread suspended in mid-air."}]'
)

moved = pipe(prompt=edit_prompt, image=knight_image, generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(0), output="images")[0]

Base model and quantized variants

Base model

Everything above uses the distilled checkpoint. The base checkpoint runs 50 steps with classifier-free guidance, and it's the one to fine-tune (see LoRA finetuning).

pipe = ModularPipeline.from_pretrained("black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein-base")
pipe.load_components(dtype={"vae": torch.float32, "default": torch.bfloat16})
pipe.to("cuda")

pipe.guider = pipe.guider.new(guidance_scale=5.0)  # optional
image = pipe(prompt=prompt, output="images")[0]

Single-file format checkpoints

Black Forest Labs also ships the transformer as a single file, in 

bf16
and in two quantized formats: 
fp8r
(rowwise FP8) and 
nvfp4
. Load any of them with 
from_single_file
, then load the other components by name so the bf16 transformer isn't downloaded too.
from diffusers import BFLQuantizationConfig, Flux3Transformer2DModel, ModularPipeline

model_id = "black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein-base"
variant = "fp8r"  # or "nvfp4"

transformer = Flux3Transformer2DModel.from_single_file(
    f"https://huggingface.co/{model_id}/blob/main/variants/{variant}/model.safetensors",
    config=model_id,
    subfolder="transformer",
    quantization_config=BFLQuantizationConfig(compute_dtype=torch.bfloat16),
    dtype=torch.bfloat16,
)

pipe = ModularPipeline.from_pretrained(model_id)
pipe.load_components(dtype=torch.bfloat16)
pipe.update_components(transformer=transformer)
pipe.to("cuda")

For the unquantized single file, use 

https://huggingface.co/{model_id}/blob/main/model.safetensors
and drop 
quantization_config
.
VariantFast kernels onOther GPUs
fp8r
 Compute capability 8.9+ (Ada, Hopper, Blackwell)Weights are dequantized each step: lower memory, no speedup
nvfp4
 Blackwell, with 
flashinfer-python
and 
flashinfer-cubin
at the same version		 Same as above

LoRA finetuning

FLUX.3 works for both text-to-image and image-to-image, which makes it a great base for custom LoRAs. 

diffusers
ships DreamBooth LoRA training scripts for both tasks (you can also train with Ostris' AI Toolkit).

Here is a text-to-image example that learns a tarot-card style from the 

multimodalart/1920-raider-waite-tarot-public-domain
dataset, triggered with 

trtcrd
:
accelerate launch train_dreambooth_lora_flux3_klein.py \
  --pretrained_model_name_or_path="black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein-base" \
  --dataset_name="multimodalart/1920-raider-waite-tarot-public-domain" \
  --caption_column="caption" \
  --instance_prompt="trtcrd" \
  --output_dir="trained-flux3-tarot-lora" \
  --mixed_precision="bf16" \
  --resolution=1024 \
  --use_aspect_ratio_buckets \
  --train_batch_size=1 \
  --rank=16 \
  --lora_alpha=16 \
  --learning_rate=1e-4 \
  --lr_scheduler="constant" \
  --max_train_steps=1500 \
  --validation_prompt="a trtcrd of a cat, tarot style" \
  --validation_epochs=25 \
  --seed=0 \
  --push_to_hub

To reduce memory usage, add a few optimization flags:

  --gradient_checkpointing \
  --cache_latents \
  --use_8bit_adam


--gradient_checkpointing
recomputes activations in the backward pass (lower VRAM, slightly slower), 
--cache_latents
pre-encodes the images and frees the VAE, and 
--use_8bit_adam
keeps the optimizer states in 8-bit.

A couple of knobs are worth experimenting with. The grid below trains the same tarot style with different LoRA ranks and optimizers; the adapters are on the Hub at 

diffusers-modular/flux3-tarot-lora
. More training features and configurations are documented in the DreamBooth FLUX.3 README.

For instruction-based editing, the image-to-image script (

train_dreambooth_lora_flux3_klein_img2img.py
) trains on (reference image, target image, instruction) triplets, where the reference is addressed in the prompt as
.

See the DreamBooth FLUX.3 README for all options and the full image-to-image example.

What it costs to run

In this section, we will talk about the memory consumption and the speed of generation of the models.

Memory

nvfp4 (RTX6000)13.415.3
fp8r (H100)14.3516.27
bf16 (H100)18.8020.72

If you have less memory:

  • Load a quantized transformer.
  • Run the text encoder separately and free it. It only runs once per image, before denoising (see Encode once, generate many).
  • Turn on automatic CPU offloading, which moves each component to the GPU only while it runs (we didn't benchmark this)
from diffusers import ComponentsManager, ModularPipeline

manager = ComponentsManager()
manager.enable_auto_cpu_offload(device="cuda")

pipe = ModularPipeline.from_pretrained("black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein", components_manager=manager)
pipe.load_components(dtype={"vae": torch.float32, "default": torch.bfloat16})
# no pipe.to("cuda"): the manager handles device placement

Speed

End-to-end timings for the distilled checkpoint (16 steps), averaged over three runs after a warmup:

WorkflowOutput sizeTimePeak memory
Text-to-image1024 × 10241.93 s23.8 GiB
Image-to-image, one 1024 × 1024 reference1024 × 10243.87 s23.8 GiB
Layout editing (the knight), one 1360 × 768 reference1360 × 7684.10 s23.8 GiB

Single NVIDIA H100 80GB, no offloading, default attention backend.

A reference image roughly doubles the time. Reference tokens join the same sequence as the text and the image being generated, so a 1024 × 1024 reference adds 4,096 tokens to every transformer call

Stacked bars of tokens per transformer call: text-to-image 4,256 tokens; image-to-image 8,272; layout text-to-image 4,336; layout image-to-image 8,800

The architecture

Let's open the model up, one piece at a time. The model takes three kinds of tokens:

  • text
  • the noisy image being generated
  • and optional reference images

From pixels to tokens

FLUX.3 is a latent-space flow model for image generation. This means that the denoiser takes latents as inputs and produces latents as outputs. We use a VAE to decode the latents back to pixels. FLUX.3 uses the same VAE architecture as Flux.2.

The FLUX.2 VAE compresses an image 8× in each direction into 32 channels, and then every 2 × 2 patch of that latent is packed into a single token with 128 channels.

So one token covers a 16 × 16 pixel patch, and a 1024 × 1024 image becomes a 64 × 64 grid of 4,096 tokens. The noisy image starts as random noise of exactly that shape. A reference image goes through the same VAE encoder and packing, and keeps its own size.

From prompt to tokens

The text encoder is Qwen3-VL, a vision-language model. FLUX.3 doesn't just take its last layer. It reads the hidden states of eight of its 36 layers (layers 4, 8, …, 32) and stacks them, so each text token becomes a 8 × 2560 = 20,480-dimensional vector before a linear layer projects it to the transformer's width of 3072.

This gives the transformer features from several depths of the language model, not just its final layer. The prompt is padded to a multiple of 80 tokens, and the transformer attends to the padding too, which is why the pipeline takes one prompt per call.

Two stages

The transformer processes the tokens in two stages:

  • Stage 1: per-mode blocks. Each stream goes through 5 blocks with its own weights. Text has its own blocks, the noisy image has its own, and the reference images have their own.
  • Stage 2: joint blocks. The streams are concatenated into one sequence, 
    [text | image | reference]
    , which goes through 28 blocks that share one set of weights.

The two stages differ in who can attend to whom.

In stage 1, each stream only attends to itself, so each kind of token gets refined on its own terms first. In stage 2, everything attends to everything, where the image learns from the text and from the references. For comparison, FLUX.2's double-stream blocks also give text and image separate weights, but let them attend to each other from the start. FLUX.3 keeps the streams fully apart first, then merges them.

At the end, the text and reference tokens are simply dropped. Only the image tokens go through the output layers, which predict how to move them one step toward a clean image.

Inside one block

Every block, in either stage, has the same shape. Attention and the MLP run in parallel on the same normalized input, and their sum is added back to the residual stream.

Each block starts with a LayerNorm that has no learned scale or shift of its own. The scale, shift, and gate come from a timestep embedding instead (this is called modulation). Inside the attention, the queries and keys are RMS-normalized and get rotary position embeddings (RoPE), which we look at below.

In a joint block, all tokens share the same weights, but text, image, and reference tokens each get their own scale, shift, and gate.

def block(x, shift, scale, gate):      # shift, scale, gate come from the token's timestep embedding
    h = layer_norm(x)                  # no learned scale or shift
    h = (1 + scale) * h + shift
    q, k, v = to_q(h), to_k(h), to_v(h)
    q, k = rope(rms_norm(q)), rope(rms_norm(k))
    out = attention(q, k, v) + mlp(h)  # parallel, MLP is SwiGLU
    return x + gate * out

Every token gets its own timestep

In FLUX.1 and FLUX.2, one timestep embedding modulates every token. In FLUX.3, the modulation depends on the kind of token.

The noisy image tokens are modulated by the current timestep 

t
. The text and reference tokens are always modulated by timestep 0, which means "clean, nothing to denoise here". So even a reference that looks almost the same as the output is marked as given context, not as something to generate.

The distilled checkpoint is a flow map. It is also told the timestep each step jumps to. That second timestep gets its own embedding, which is added to every token's modulation, so each of its 16 steps can make a larger jump.

Positions in four dimensions

Attention on its own doesn't know where a token is (this phenomenon is called permutation equivariance). RoPE fixes that by rotating each query and key by an amount that depends on the token's position. FLUX.3 uses four position axes, 

(t, h, w, l)
(timestep, height, width, length of sequence), and gives each one a quarter (32 dimensions) of every 128-dimensional attention head:
Tokenst: timesteph: heightw: widthl: length of sequence
text token i000i
image token at (row, col)0row / 2col / 20
reference k at (row, col)0row / 2col / 2−(k + 1)

Text tokens line up along 

l
, like words in a sentence. The image and the references are 2D grids in 
(h, w)
, separated from each other along 
l
. Because a reference uses the same 
(h, w)
coordinates as the output, "the same spot in the reference" has a precise meaning to the model, which is what the 
src_bbox
/ 
tgt_bbox
editing relies on.

The denoising loop

FLUX.3 is a flow-matching model. Generation starts from pure noise, and at each of the 50 steps the transformer predicts a velocity. This is the direction from noise toward a clean image. The scheduler takes one step along it.

At every step you can also read off the model's current guess of the final image. Decoding that guess at a few steps shows how the image takes shape:

The fox, its pose, and the light are already in place by step 10, while the noise level is still 0.97. The snow-laden branches and the texture of the fur only appear in the last few steps. FLUX.3's scheduler uses a large time shift (6.93), which keeps the noise level high for most of the run: 44 of the 50 steps happen above σ = 0.5. We built this figure by adding one small block to the pipeline, which brings us to Modular Diffusers.

If you are new to flow matching, we have a beginner friendly tutorial and a video for you to understand how it works.

Modular Diffusers

FLUX.3 ships as a Modular Diffusers pipeline.

See the workflows

You can list the workflows and print the exact blocks of each one, without loading any weights.

from diffusers import Flux3AutoBlocks

blocks = Flux3AutoBlocks()
print(blocks.available_workflows)
# ['text2image', 'image_conditioned']

print(list(blocks.get_workflow("text2image").sub_blocks))
# ['text_encoder', 'denoise.input', 'denoise.prepare_latents', 'denoise.set_timesteps',
#  'denoise.prepare_rope_inputs', 'denoise.denoise', 'denoise.after_denoise', 'decode']


get_workflow()
resolves the auto branches and gives you the plain sequence of steps that will run. 
print(blocks.get_workflow("image_conditioned").doc)
prints the components, inputs, defaults, and outputs of that workflow.

Encode once, generate many

Pop the text encoder out, encode the prompt once, free it, and generate from the cached embeddings.

import torch
from diffusers import ModularPipeline

model_id = "black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein-base"

blocks = ModularPipeline.from_pretrained(model_id).blocks
text_blocks = blocks.sub_blocks.pop("text_encoder")  # `blocks` now starts at the VAE encoder

text_pipe = text_blocks.init_pipeline(model_id)
text_pipe.load_components(dtype=torch.bfloat16)
text_pipe.to("cuda")

state = text_pipe(prompt=prompt, negative_prompt="")  # no guider here, so ask for the negative embeddings

prompt_embeds = state.get("prompt_embeds")
negative_prompt_embeds = state.get("negative_prompt_embeds")

del text_pipe
torch.cuda.empty_cache()

image_pipe = blocks.init_pipeline(model_id)  # no text encoder to load
image_pipe.load_components(dtype={"vae": torch.float32, "default": torch.bfloat16})
image_pipe.to("cuda")

for seed in range(3):
    image = image_pipe(
        prompt_embeds=prompt_embeds,
        negative_prompt_embeds=negative_prompt_embeds,
        generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(seed),
        output="images",
    )[0]
    image.save(f"{seed}.png")

Add a step inside the loop

The denoising figure above came from one extra block that records the model's guess of the clean image at every step:

from diffusers.modular_pipelines import Flux3AutoBlocks, InputParam, ModularPipelineBlocks, OutputParam


class Flux3PreviewStep(ModularPipelineBlocks):
    model_name = "flux3"

    @property
    def inputs(self):
        return [InputParam("latents"), InputParam("noise_pred")]

    @property
    def intermediate_outputs(self):
        return [OutputParam("x0_previews", type_hint=list)]

    @torch.no_grad()
    def __call__(self, components, block_state, i, t):
        if i == 0:
            block_state.x0_previews = []
        sigma = t / 1000  # timesteps are sigmas scaled to [0, 1000]
        block_state.x0_previews.append(block_state.latents - sigma * block_state.noise_pred)  # x0 = x_t - sigma * v
        return components, block_state


blocks = Flux3AutoBlocks()
denoise_loop = blocks.sub_blocks["denoise"].sub_blocks["text2image"].sub_blocks["denoise"]
denoise_loop.sub_blocks.insert("preview", Flux3PreviewStep(), 1)  # between "denoiser" and "after_denoiser"

pipe = blocks.init_pipeline(model_id)
pipe.load_components(dtype={"vae": torch.float32, "default": torch.bfloat16})
pipe.to("cuda")

out = pipe(prompt=prompt, generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(0), output=["x0_previews", "images"])

Try it

  • Models: FLUX.3 Image Klein collection
  • Docs: FLUX.3 in Diffusers
  • Fine-tune: DreamBooth LoRA scripts
  • Prompting: Black Forest Labs prompting guide

Built something with FLUX.3? Share your LoRAs and pipelines on the Hub. We'd love to see them! 😎

entries.title: HiRO-ACEv2: Simulating extreme weather at 3 km resolution for a fraction of the cost
entries.content:
allenai/HiRO-ACEv2

Updated • 4

HiRO-ACEv2: Simulating extreme weather at 3 km resolution for a fraction of the cost

Enterprise Article

Models| 📄

Paper| 📓

Tutorial notebooks| 🌎

Demo

We introduce HiRO-ACEv2, the newest update to our High Resolution Output Ai2 Climate Emulator (HiRO-ACE) system. HiROv2 can reproduce even extremely rare rain, wind, and pressure events with high accuracy, while the full system can generate global 3 km climate data at about 1/300th the cost of X-SHiELD, a high-resolution global atmospheric model that explicitly simulates storms and other small-scale weather.

HiRO-ACE, introduced earlier in 2026, has two parts: ACE, an AI model that operates at a coarser 100 km resolution, and HiRO, a model that sharpens those coarse outputs into fine 3 km detail. The biggest change in HiRO-ACEv2 is the new downscaling model, HiROv2, which can now 1) predict several high-resolution fields at once instead of just rainfall, so it can capture a much wider range of extreme weather, and 2) has improved skill in predicting extreme events.

Our main focus with HiRO-ACEv2 was to simulate extreme events well. Changes to how we train HiROv2 improved its ability to reproduce the most intense rain, wind, and pressure values. When given coarsened X-SHiELD data, it matches the target simulation's high-resolution statistics to within 3%, even for events so rare they occur only once in a million data points. It also accurately estimates the total energy of tropical cyclones, including storms it never saw during training, and generates hurricanes with realistic eyes and rain bands, though winds and pressure around the eye remain somewhat more lopsided than in X-SHiELD. Additionally, HiROv2 realistically generates strong winds flowing down mountain slopes.

We also trained an updated version of ACE for this system. Over a 10-year simulation, its hurricanes, average climate patterns, and overall distributions of rain, wind, and pressure all line up well with X-SHiELD. That tells us ACE's coarse simulations are a solid foundation for producing long-term high-resolution climate data.

Putting HiROv2 and ACE together, we generated a full year of global 3 km data. Its statistics closely match X-SHiELD's, even though HiRO was working from a simulation ACE ran on its own rather than from real X-SHiELD data. Across a 10-year run, the energy of HiRO-ACEv2's hurricanes is comparable to X-SHiELD's over the same period, and snapshots from that run show a variety of other extreme events that resemble those in X-SHiELD.

An example of a strong hurricane in the North Atlantic, generated during the 10-year HiRO-ACEv2 simulation.

Overall, HiRO-ACEv2 offers researchers a flexible and inexpensive way to generate many versions of high-resolution rain, wind, and pressure data for extreme events over 10 years or more. Producing global high-resolution data with it costs roughly 300 times less than running X-SHiELD. If only one region is needed, the savings can be more than a hundred times greater, depending on the size of the area. We're also working on a streamlined version of HiROv2 that could make it more than ten times faster still.

We still have future work ahead of us: because HiRO learned from X-SHiELD, it only works with the version of ACE tuned to match X-SHiELD. That means it can't yet produce high-resolution data for other climates, such as a warmer future or the historical record in datasets like ERA5. Next, we plan to train on new X-SHiELD datasets, including one simulating a world 4°C warmer, so the system can handle different climates. We also plan to add outputs like near-surface temperature and snow and ice, which would allow for even more uses, such as snowpack prediction.

Visualizing and using HiRO outputs

Simulated 10 m wind speed over Baja California in the ACE data visualizer: ACE2 at 100 km resolution on the main map and HiRO-ACEv2 at 3 km in the inset.

A simulated storm over the northeastern Pacific in the ACE data visualizer. The main map shows 10 m wind speed at 100 km resolution; the 3 km HiRO-ACEv2 inset shows finer structure within the storm.

To make it easy to see what HiRO produces without running any inference, we built a web demo that shows pre-generated precipitation, wind, and sea-level pressure output from HiROv1 and HiROv2 side by side with X-SHiELD, the simulation they were trained on. The demo complements the quantitative comparisons in our tech report: it offers a quick visual check of how the outputs look, and lets users zoom in on their own region of interest to judge performance there.

For more in-depth analysis, the models are available to download, and our tutorial notebooks walk through how to run them.

entries.title: Run fast, private agents on-device with LFM2.5-24B-A2B
entries.content:
LiquidAI/LFM2-24B-A2B

Text Generation • 24B • Updated • 2.92k • 356

Run fast, private agents on-device with LFM2.5-24B-A2B

Team Article

LFM2.5-24B-A2Bis a 24B-parameter reasoning model with just 2B active parameters, built for fast, private agents on-device. It thinks before it answers, calls tools, and works through multi-step tasks inside popular agent harnesses. Because only 2B parameters are active per token, each reasoning token is cheap, so you can run agents continuously on your own hardware.

  • Best-in-class agent: Competitive with Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, a model with ~50% more total and active parameters, on agentic and tool-use tasks, scoring 48.09 on LiveClaw versus 38.19.
  • Reasoning at MoE speed: Always thinks before it answers. With only 2B active parameters per token, each reasoning token is cheap.
  • Efficient inference: 184 tok/s on an Apple M5 Max and up to 21K output tok/s on a single NVIDIA B300 GPU.

How we built a reasoning agent with 2B active parameters

LFM2.5-24B-A2B builds on LFM2-24B-A2B and keeps its architecture: 40 layers, 64 experts per MoE block with top-4 routing, and the same hybrid of gated short convolutions and GQA. The context window grows from 32K to 131K tokens, and an in-place tokenizer expansion doubles the vocabulary from 65K to 128K tokens for better non-Latin tokenization. Unlike its predecessor, it is a reasoning-only model that produces an explicit chain of thought before its final answer.

Pre-training was scaled up from ~17T to ~33T tokens. Mid-training then adds 2T tokens at 32K context, weighted toward reasoning, math, code, instruction following, and multilingual text, and 300B tokens at 131K context, weighted toward long-context data. Tool calls and multi-turn trajectories appear throughout both phases. Post-training turns the base model into an agent in five stages:

  • Supervised fine-tuning (SFT)
  • Teacher specialization
  • Multi-domain on-policy distillation (MOPD), non-agentic: distill the specialist teachers on non-agentic tasks.
  • MOPD, agentic: a second distillation stage focused on agentic tasks.
  • Agentic reinforcement learning (Agentic RL): train the model inside agent harnesses, such as OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, Pi, and OpenCode.

Benchmark results

We evaluated LFM2.5-24B-A2B against Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it, and Nemotron-3.5-Lightning on 16 benchmarks covering tool use and agentic workflows, knowledge, instruction following, math, and coding. It is the smallest model in the group, yet it is competitive with MoEs with ~50% more total and active parameters.

BenchmarkLFM2.5-24B-A2BQwen3.6-35B-A3BGemma-4-26B-A4B-itNemotron-3.5-Lightning (30B-A3B)

*All the models were evaluated with vLLM, using each benchmark's recommended generation parameters.

For your app, the strengths are tool use and instruction following. LFM2.5-24B-A2B leads or matches the competition on five of the eight tool-use and agentic benchmarks (AutomationBench, BFCLv4, ToolSandbox, LiveClaw, and τ³-Bench Banking), and on AutomationBench it scores more than three times the next-best model. It also leads on all three instruction-following benchmarks. Larger models keep an edge on knowledge-heavy benchmarks like GPQA Diamond, HLE, and AA-Omniscience, and on coding benchmarks like SWE-Bench Verified (OpenCode) and SciCode, so pair LFM2.5-24B-A2B with retrieval or web search for knowledge-heavy workloads.

These results make LFM2.5-24B-A2B a strong foundation for agents that need to reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device.

Inference speed on CPU and GPU

LFM2.5-24B-A2B ships with day-one support across the inference ecosystem, including llama.cpp, MLX, vLLM, SGLang, and ONNX.

Edge inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest of the compared MoEs, decoding 184 tokens/s on an M5 Max and 114 tokens/s on a Ryzen AI Max+ 395. That is up to 1.7x faster than the next-best model, while using the least memory.

GPU inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest model in its size class, reaching over 21K output tokens per second at high concurrency on a single B300.

How to use LFM2.5-24B-A2B

Reach for LFM2.5-24B-A2B when you need agents that reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device.

Install the latest version of 

transformers
(compatible with 
transformers>=5.0.0
):
pip install -U transformers

Then load and run the model:

from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer, TextStreamer

model_id = "LiquidAI/LFM2.5-24B-A2B"
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    model_id,
    device_map="auto",
    dtype="bfloat16",
#   attn_implementation="flash_attention_2" <- uncomment on compatible GPU
)
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id)
streamer = TextStreamer(tokenizer, skip_prompt=True, skip_special_tokens=True)

prompt = "What is C. elegans?"

input_ids = tokenizer.apply_chat_template(
    [{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
    add_generation_prompt=True,
    return_tensors="pt",
    tokenize=True,
)["input_ids"].to(model.device)

output = model.generate(
    input_ids,
    do_sample=True,
    temperature=0.1,
    top_k=50,
    repetition_penalty=1.05,
    max_new_tokens=512,
    streamer=streamer,
)

Use it in your agent harness

Serve LFM2.5-24B-A2B locally behind any OpenAI-compatible backend, then point your agent harness at it. For example, with Hermes Agent:

hermes config set model.provider custom
hermes config set model.base_url http://localhost:8080/v1
hermes config set model.default LFM2.5-24B-A2B
hermes config set model.context_length 131072
hermes config set model.api_mode chat_completions
hermes config set agent.tool_use_enforcement true

The port depends on your serving backend: llama.cpp and MLX use 

8080
, vLLM uses 
8000
, SGLang uses 
30000
, and LM Studio uses 
1234
. See the model card for OpenClaw and Pi configs, and our guide for the full setup. Check out our release blog for video examples.

Get Started with LFM2.5-24B-A2B

Both LFM2.5-24B-A2B and LFM2.5-24B-A2B-Base are open-weight and available on Hugging Face today:

  • Download: LFM2.5-24B-A2B-Base and LFM2.5-24B-A2B on Hugging Face.
  • Use in your harness: follow our guide on how to run a local agent, like OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, and Pi.
  • Fine-tune: adapt LFM2.5-24B-A2B to your task with our fine-tuning tutorials.

We can't wait to see what you build.
